search_source.Keywords: solidification     Soldering     Micromechanical Testing     Extreme Temperatures     Marangoni Convection     Microstructure Characterization     Porosity
search_source.SubResearch Area: Microstructural Characterization, Terrestrial vs Microgravity Effects, Solder Joints
search_source.Proposal Title: Structure, Properties, and Performance of Solder Joints in Terrestrial vs. Reduced-Gravity Environments
search_source.Objectives: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.
search_source.Approach:
The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu.
Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.
search_source.Hypothesis: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives:

(i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.

search_source.Title: Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment-1
search_source.Keywords: USML-1     STDCE-1     thermocapillary flow     buoyancy     Columbia     Surface Tension     Constant Flux     Marangoni Number
search_source.Objectives:
The main objectives of STDCE-1 are to investigate:
    -The extent and nature of thermocapillary flows in transient periods as well as under steady conditions.
    -Temperature distributions along the free surface and in the bulk fluid.
    -The effect of the heating mode and the heating level on the flows.
    -The effect of the liquid free surface on the flows
    -The onset conditions and nature of oscillatory flows
search_source.Approach:
The STDCE program employed a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to investigate the complexities of thermocapillary flow. This strategy encompassed a combination of theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, ground-based experiments, and ultimately, microgravity experiments aboard the Space Shuttle.

Theoretical Analysis
   Dimensionless Parameters: Researchers derived and identified the key dimensionless parameters governing thermocapillary flow, including the Marangoni number (Ma), Prandtl number (Pr), aspect ratio (Ar), and the novel surface deformation parameter (S). These parameters facilitated the understanding of the relative importance of different forces and physical mechanisms at play and provided a framework for data analysis and comparison.

   Scaling Laws: By analyzing the governing equations and boundary conditions, scientists established scaling laws that characterized the behavior of key flow features, such as boundary layer thicknesses and velocity scales. This theoretical groundwork offered valuable insights into the expected flow characteristics under different conditions.

Numerical Modeling
   Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD): Sophisticated CFD models were developed to simulate thermocapillary flow behavior under various conditions. These models accounted for factors such as heat transfer, fluid properties, surface tension effects, and free surface deformation. The numerical simulations provided detailed predictions of flow patterns, velocity distributions, and temperature profiles, serving as a basis for comparison with experimental data and for exploring a wider range of parameters than feasible experimentally.

Ground-Based Experiments
   Reduced-Gravity Simulations: Researchers conducted experiments in drop towers and other reduced-gravity facilities to observe thermocapillary flows under conditions with minimized buoyancy effects. These experiments served as a stepping stone towards the microgravity experiments and provided preliminary data for model validation and refinement.

   Test Fluid and Hardware Development: Extensive ground-based testing was undertaken to optimize the experimental setup, including the selection of the test fluid (silicone oil), the design of the test cell, and the development of flow visualization and temperature measurement techniques.

Microgravity Experiments
   Space Shuttle Missions: The culmination of the research effort involved conducting the STDCE experiments aboard the Space Shuttle, taking advantage of the extended microgravity environment to study thermocapillary flows over a broader range of parameters and conditions than possible on Earth. This included meticulous execution of the test matrix, encompassing various heating modes, power levels, and free surface shapes, while collecting detailed flow visualization and temperature data.

Data Analysis and Model Validation
   Comparison of Results: The experimental data from both ground-based and microgravity experiments were rigorously analyzed and compared with the predictions from numerical models. This iterative process allowed for the assessment of model accuracy, the identification of areas for improvement, and ultimately, a deeper understanding of the fundamental physics driving thermocapillary flow.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
While the STDCE program was primarily driven by the need to understand and predict thermocapillary flow behavior in microgravity environments, its findings and technological advancements have yielded valuable insights and applications for Earth-based processes as well.

Enhanced Understanding of Thermocapillary Flows
Fundamental Physics: STDCE significantly advanced the understanding of the fundamental physics governing thermocapillary flows, including the interplay between surface tension gradients, heat transfer, and fluid motion. This knowledge provides a solid foundation for tackling complex fluid flow problems in various terrestrial applications.

Numerical Model Refinement: The experimental data from STDCE served as a critical benchmark for validating and refining numerical models used to predict thermocapillary flow behavior. These improved models now offer more accurate and reliable predictions for a wider range of applications, both in space and on Earth.

Technological Advancements
Non-Intrusive Measurement Techniques: The development and refinement of non-intrusive measurement techniques, such as infrared imaging and particle image velocimetry, for the STDCE have expanded the toolkit for studying fluid flows in various settings. These techniques are now widely employed in research and industrial applications on Earth, including the study of combustion processes, crystal growth, and microfluidics.

Flow Visualization and Analysis: The advanced flow visualization and analysis methods developed for STDCE have facilitated the study of complex flow patterns and structures in various terrestrial applications. These tools enable researchers and engineers to gain deeper insights into flow dynamics and optimize processes for improved efficiency and performance.

Earth-Based Applications
Materials Processing: The insights gained from STDCE have direct relevance to materials processing techniques on Earth, particularly those involving free surfaces and high-temperature gradients, such as welding, crystal growth, and the fabrication of thin films and coatings. Understanding and controlling thermocapillary flows in these processes can lead to improved product quality and reduced defect formation.

Microfluidics: The knowledge gained from STDCE is applicable to the burgeoning field of microfluidics, where surface tension forces play a dominant role in manipulating and controlling fluids at the microscale. This has implications for the development of microfluidic devices for applications such as drug delivery, medical diagnostics, and chemical analysis.

Overall, the STDCE program, while initially motivated by the challenges of microgravity research, has generated valuable knowledge and technological advancements with far-reaching implications for various Earth-based applications. The enhanced understanding of thermocapillary flow and the development of advanced measurement and analysis techniques have contributed to the advancement of materials processing, microfluidics, and numerous other fields, demonstrating the profound impact of fundamental scientific research on both space exploration and terrestrial technology.

search_source.Title: In Space Soldering Investigation
search_source.Keywords: In-Space Soldering     Microgravity     surface tension gradient     Welding     porosity     kinematic and dynamic viscosity
search_source.Objectives: The primary objective is to better understand the quality of solders in a microgravity environment.  In microgravity, gas bubbles, or void spaces are found in the solder joint and at contact surfaces.  These voids reduce the thermal and electrical conductivity and also provide sites for crack initiation.  Bubbles have less chance to escape in the reduced gravity environment of space. Hence, by designing a systematic series of simple experiments, the objective was to investigate and better understand porosity development, surface wetting, and equilibrium shape formation while soldering in a reduced gravity environment.
search_source.Approach: The proposed experiments basically consisted of taking pieces of silver-coated copper wire and bending/twisting them into simple configurations for test coupons. Selected lengths of Kester “44”® 60-40 rosin core solder (5 and 10 cm) were then cut and wrapped around a selected portion of the coupon, to be later melted by heat conduction through the wire using the kit’s soldering iron. A second set of experiments involved feeding 5 and 10 cm lengths of solder onto similar shaped coupons that were being heated by the iron. In principle, the soldering iron was never meant to come in contact with the molten solder. All in all, five soldering sessions were conducted on the ISS that culminated in 86 samples comprising seven different wire configurations, two different solder lengths (5 and 10 cm), and two different melt procedures (conduction melting of wrapped solder and conduction melting of solder being fed onto the wire). The melting experiments took place in the flame retardant Maintenance Work Area, a portable facility in the ISS used to make repairs and conduct other operations in the ISS. A digital camera is placed behind the samples to record the melting and subsequent solidification experiments. Video footage and still pictures were down linked after each experimental session.
search_source.Hypothesis: Due to minimized buoyancy in the microgravity environment, it is hypothesized that one would expect additional porosity and enhanced surface tension contributions to porosity shape and mobility. Brazing, soldering, and welding operations in microgravity can be influenced greatly by both wetting and surface tension-driven flows, primary factors in achieving or not achieving a sound joint. For example, processes that rely on gravity-driven separations in the terrestrial environment, such as the removal of gas bubbles from a liquid, may rely on completely different interfacial phenomenon in microgravity.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: An investigation of soldering practices and behavior in a microgravity environment is relevant to our technological needs, particularly with regard to in-space fabrication and repair. The ISSI payload provides unique insight into microgravity soldering methods, which could play a fundamental role in maintaining the International Space Station as well as provide understanding of repair capabilities on future missions to the Moon and to Mars. The study of soldering in space could lead to better soldering techniques here on Earth.

search_source.Objectives:
Specific objectives of this investigation were as follows:
   • Plan and develop experiment parameter sets to investigate anomalous nucleation events in zirconium samples during ISS-EML experiments
   • Analyze cavitation-induced nucleation experiments on zirconium and zirconium-nickel alloys
   • Analyze fluid flow during ISS-EML experiments to support collaborators investigations
   • Continue flight preparations and development of experimental parameter sets for upcoming experiments in Batch 3
   • Provide magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) modeling support of macroconvection in various materials for three ESA sponsored projects: PARSEC, THERMOLAB - ISS, ICOPROSOL.
search_source.Approach:
• The anomalous nucleation events of interest are hypothesized to be caused by cavitation in the melt. Experiments replicated the conditions in which the nucleation events were previously observed and explored similar experimental conditions.
• Magnetohydrodynamic modeling of fluid flow is to be used to determine the flow conditions during ISS-EML experiments. Relevant parameters include fluid velocity, shear rates, turbulence intensity, and their distribution. Such data is critical for control of experiments and input to other theoretical and modeling efforts.
search_source.Hypothesis:
• Dynamic nucleation is an effect of the fluid flow and not reliant on classical nucleation theory.
• Thermophysical property measurements may require appropriate flow conditions, which should be quantified
• Flow conditions may affect solidification and nucleation behavior
• Oxygen may influence surface tension measurements in metallic melts
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Containerless processing provides access to the deeply undercooled region of metallic melts. Using this unique processing environement we are able to investigate fundamental solidification behaivor and meausure thermophysical properties of metallic melts including density, surface tension, viscosity, thermal expansion, heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and electrical conductivity. More specifically, impacts and benefits are broken out by the 3 associated flight experiments.

In PARSEC,  the effect of fluid flow on the solidification path of certain alloys is investigated. Control of the solidification path would enable tailoring of the microstructure and properties of metal parts for specific applications.

In ThermoLAB, the thermophysical properties of high-temperature materials is investigated. Many of these materials are used commercially. A better understanding of the physical properties will allow more efficient and more reliable production of metallic parts using these alloys. Other alloys are chosen because of scientific interest in their properties, which may illuminate fundamental physics related to the formation of bulk metallic glasses and quasicrystals.

The nucleation and growth of quasicrystals, and the effect of atomic-scale order on the macroscopic properties of these alloys is investigated in ICOPROSOL. This fundamental investigation may improve our ability to tailor the microstructure of metals for commercial applications.

search_source.Title: Capillary Flow Experiment
search_source.Keywords: Capillary Flow Experiment (CFE)     Capillary forces     CFE
search_source.Objectives:
1. The primary objective of the CL unit experiments is to identify the extent the role of the boundary condition at the contact line plays in the natural dynamic response of a large capillary interface to a variety of disturbances.
2. The primary objective of the ICF units is to experimentally determine secondary imbibition rates in complex containers due to spontaneous large length scale capillary flows along interior corners in weakly 3-dimensional containers. Secondary objectives of the experiments are to quantify such flows in closed loop cycles, and to identify the passive phase separation characteristics of certain capillary driven multiphase-flows (e.g. bubbly flow) along interior corners.
3. The primary objective of the VG units is to determine equilibrium interface configurations and critical wetting conditions for interfaces between interior corners separated by a gap. A secondary objective is to validate numerical predictions of the large length scale discontinuous or nearly discontinuous wetting phenomena.
search_source.Approach: Without gravity, it is more difficult to control the flow of fluids and this is a challenge for designing spacecraft systems such as liquid propellants/cryogens, thermal control systems, wastewater management and recycling.Capillary forces (the interaction of liquid with solid that can draw a fluid up a narrow tube) continue to act in the absence of gravity and can be exploited to control fluid orientation so that fluid systems on spacecraft perform predictably.CFE uses the low-gravity environment provided by the International Space Station to understand the special dynamics of capillary flow and will aid in the design of fluid transport systems on future spacecraft.
search_source.Hypothesis: The CFE investigations operate under the hypothesis that capillary phenomena in microgravity, specifically contact line dynamics, interior corner flows, and vane-gap wetting, deviate significantly from idealized theoretical predictions based on simplified geometries and boundary conditions. This deviation is anticipated to manifest as measurable differences in dynamic interface response (frequency and damping) for varying contact line conditions, geometry-dependent secondary imbibition rates in complex containers, and distinct critical wetting conditions in vane-wall gaps influenced by gap size and wettability. The CFE experiments are designed to quantify these deviations, providing empirical data to refine existing theoretical models and enhance the predictive capabilities for low-gravity fluid management systems.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The knowledge gained from this payload has the potential to be instrumental in the design of future fluid systems for spacecraft-impacting fluid bearing containers such as propellant and cryogenic fluids tanks, thermal control system coolant reservoirs, water storage and management systems, liquid state low-gravity materials processing equipment, and biofluids handling instruments for inflight human health systems. By performing this experiment, researchers will gain information that will lead to improvements in system reliability with reductions in system mass and complexity. These applications of CFE are in direct support of NASA's mission to develop safe, reliable, and affordable spacecraft to pursue the greater exploration of our solar system and universe. The results of the flight experiments are also expected to provide insights into terrestrial interfacial phenomena and may lead to models predicting fluid flows in porous media (i.e. ground water transport), complex capillary structures (i.e. high performance wicks for heat pipes employed in electronics cooling), and Lab-On-Chip technologies (i.e., microscale biofluids processing).

search_source.Title: Capillary Flow Experiment - 2
search_source.Keywords: CFE     Capillary forces     Capillary Flow Experiment (CFE)     CFE-2
search_source.Objectives: Liquids behave differently in space than they do on Earth, so containers that can process, hold or transport them must be designed carefully to work in microgravity. The Capillary Flow Experiment-2 furthers research on wetting, which is a liquid’s ability to spread across a surface, and its impact over large length scales in strange container shapes in microgravity environments. This work will improve our capabilities to quickly and accurately predict how related processes occur, and allow us to design better systems to process liquids aboard spacecraft (i.e., liquid fuel tanks, thermals fluids, and water processing for life support).
search_source.Approach: Wetting describes how well a liquid is attracted to a solid surface. Understanding the impact of wetting over large length scales in microgravity is important for a wide variety of engineering systems being developed for human spaceflight.Studies from CFE-2 may serve to demonstrate how liquids can be efficiently and passively separated from gases in the absence of gravity. This is a key operation in fluid systems aboard spacecraft such as water purification systems for life support.
search_source.Hypothesis: This research hypothesizes that capillary flows in microgravity are strongly influenced by container geometry, particularly interior corners and gaps. For vane gaps, a critical wetting condition, dependent on gap size and vane design, is expected. In interior corners, imbibition rates, phase separation, and bubble dynamics should be highly sensitive to 3D geometry, with long-duration microgravity being crucial for observing subtle, slow processes. Experiments are designed to quantify these relationships and validate theoretical models.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The Capillary Flow Experiments demonstrate how capillary forces work in space, how differently shaped containers change the wicking behavior of a wetting fluid, and how such can be used to passively separate liquids and gases.  Understanding how microgravity amplifies these behaviors could improve the reliability of such key processes as water purification fuel storage and supply, and general liquid transport aboard spacecraft. On Earth capillary action allows small amounts of liquid to flow up and into tight spaces despite the effects of gravity. search_source.Objectives:
OASIS studies the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity, including their overall motion and the merging of crystal layers known as smectic islands. Liquid crystals are used for display screens in televisions and clocks, and they also occur in soaps and in cell membranes. The experiment allows detailed studies of the behavior of these structures, and how microgravity affects their unique ability to act like both a liquid and a solid crystal.
The specific research objectives are:
    -To exploit the unique characteristics of freely suspended liquid crystals in a microgravity environment to advance the understanding of fluid state physics.
    -Study basic 2D hydrodynamics/fluid physics, probe droplet/island diffusion, hydrodynamic interactions, and droplet/island coalescence
search_source.Approach: The OASIS experiment’s goal is to better understand the unique behavior of liquid crystals in microgravity. OASIS observes the various aspects of liquid crystals behavior in microgravity such as overall fluid motion, diffusion (the movement of particles from an area of high concentration to low concentration) and the merging of liquid crystal film layers called islands, Fundamental studies of complex fluid physics behavior will be accomplished in two dimensional fluids using freely suspended liquid crystals. The impact of the research is to advance the understanding of two-dimensional system physics of complex fluids. Space helmets could use ferroelectric liquid crystal micro-displays. It could advance the understanding of well aligned very high speed electro-optic devices.
search_source.Hypothesis: In a microgravity environment, freely suspended smectic liquid crystal (FSLC) films will exhibit unique hydrodynamic and interfacial behaviors, such as reduced coarsening rates of island emulsions, enhanced 2D thermocapillarity effects, and distinct equilibrium spatial organization of islands, due to the absence of gravitational forces, convection, and sedimentation, enabling precise tests of theoretical models of 2D hydrodynamics and phase behavior.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Future space helmets may use certain types of liquid crystals in small display screens directly applied to the face shield where astronauts can easily view them. Understanding how liquid crystals behave in microgravity helps researchers to design liquid crystal displays (LCDs) that can perform better in space. Liquid crystals can flow like a liquid, but contain molecules that are arranged in a specific pattern, just like a crystal. Greater understanding of the physics behind these structures could lead to improved liquid crystal display devices, including devices with improved color contrast and response times. It could also advance research in high-speed electro-optic devices used to control a light beam.

search_source.Proposal Title: Round Robin: Thermophysical Property Measurement, Augmented-Program for Levitation Utilization in Space (A-PLUS)
search_source.Objectives:
The key scientific objectives are:
   (a) Conducting baseline space ESL containerless property measurement experiments for two paired classes of levitation-based thermophysical properties:Density/Thermal Expansion, Viscosity/Surface Tension.
   (b) Selecting materials compatible with both electrostatic levitation (ESL) and electromagnetic levitation (EML) to allow comparison between space facilities.
   (c) Using modeling to evaluate theories used to predict the influence of gravity on propertymeasurement experiments.
   (d) Actively encouraging collaboration with existing science teams using other facilities through organizing a Round Robin test consortium
search_source.Approach:
The experimental approach involved inserting a sample carousel of 20 individual samples into the JAXA ISS-ELF facility, conditioning the test atmosphere, and conducting individual melt cycles on each sample. The heating lasers were used to precondition the sample when the sample is heated to a desired pre-bake temperature. Following the preconditioning period, the sample was charged by the electrodes and released to achieve stable positioning. The lasers were then used to thermally cycle the sample. The cycle starts by application of the highest laser heating power (activated by a control current setting in the ELF software measured in amps) until the sample is fully molten and achieved the maximum liquid superheat temperature. The heater power was then turned down to maintain the desired isothermal hold. Surface excitation was conducted using varying volage from the electrodes at this temperature. Surface tension and viscosity was measured using the droplet oscillation behavior. The laser power was then turned off to allow the molten sample to cool down. Density and cp/ε evaluations are conducted during the free cooling without any influence from the laser. Once recalescence occurred, the sample was then allowed to become fully solid at room temperature which marks the completion of a thermal cycle. Overall, processing a single melt cycle can take up to 10 - 15 minutes excluding the pre-bake. Following the cycle completion, the sample is retrieved back into the cartridge to end the test on this sample.

Using the described experimental approach several thermophysical properties were measured on a variety of metallic melts as described below:
1.	 Density –One high-speed video camera was used to monitor the sample size as a function of time during the free cooling phase. Sample edge was detected using a custom algorithm for the density measurement. The volume of the sample was calculated using a known calibration of pixels/mm3, which was subsequently correlated with temperature allowing calculation of density and thermal expansion coefficient (from the slope of the density curve). Tracking of sample mass loss was accomplished post-mission using Langmuir’s equation of evaporation.
2.	 Surface tension – After melting, the heating laser is set to a reduced value such that the sample is held at constant temperature. A sinusoidal modulation of the positioning voltage was applied to both electrodes to excite surface oscillations without changing sample position. The resulting sample deformation was measured by the high-speed linear array. A frequeny sweep was conducted to identify natural frequency. Two method was applied to identify the natural frequency from the sweep: (1) Maximum amplitude method where maximum deformation is observed at the natural frequency and (2) Excitation crossover method where the natural frequency was observed at the linear intersections  of the damped and free oscillations.  Natural frequencies identified using both methods were used to evaluate the surface tension.
3.	Viscosity – In conjunction to surface tension, viscosity was measured from the damped oscillations at the identified natural frequency. The characteristic exponential time decay from a sinusoidal fit was used to evaluate the viscosity.
4.	Specific heat capacity and emissivity – The ratio of these two quantities was evaluated from the cooling curve as monitored by the IR pyrometer after correction for conductive mass losses to the gas environment.
5.	Evaporation – Integration of the time-temperature profile allows calculation of evaporation assuming a known relationship using Langmuir’s equation for loss as a function of temperature. Pre- and post- measurement of sample mass anchors these predictions. Dynamic mass is crucial for tracking for density, surface tension and viscosity measurement.
search_source.Hypothesis: The experimental hypothesis was that in microgravity environment in the absence of stirring, high quality thermophysical property would be measured compared to the ground-based levitation facility. This was successfully observed for gold samples.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This research aids in dissemination of an baseline archived dataset allowing researchers to validate models accounting for gravity-induced systematic error in property measurement used for industrial welding, casting  and additive manufacturing operations . Industry will be better able to correlate ground and space results to expand the quantity and quality of available information without the requirement for access to space. Advance the understanding of how to best allocate the scant resources available for space-based materials property measurement using levitation.  In the future this could lead to development of a model where fidelity and cost can be readily calculated for a given material classification and serve as the basis for prioritization of specific ground and space thermophysical property investigations.

The work comprises the application of available knowledge to the preparation and characterization of particle stabilized emulsions, produced by adapting to the Soft Matter Dynamics instrument.

Is the growth law for average bubble size R~√ time, such that R dR/dt is a constant? If so, what is the liquid-fraction dependence of this rate?
How do the rate and the nature of the bubble rearrangement dynamics change as the liquid fraction is increased to the point of un-jamming (transition solid-like to liquid-like)?

Evaluate the characteristic time for the droplet coalescence as a function of the formulation

search_source.Approach:
The PArticle STAbilised emulsions experiment (PASTA) is placed inside the Fluid Science Rack (FSL) in the European Columbus module of the ISS.
Each PASTA sample cell is fitted with a piston that allows to agitate the mixture within the cell at various frequencies and durations to emulsify the mixture. The sample cells are grouped 4-by-4 in sample cell units that can be fitted on a carousel inside SMD. This carousel allows for placing each individual sample cell in the diagnostics position of SMD, where it can be observed with the SMD sensors and several diagnostic tools, like the overview camera that takes microscope image sequences in black and white of the sample cell.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Emulsions have large relevance for applications in a wide spectrum of technologies, processes, and products in different fields including oil and gas, specialty materials, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and foods. In the food industry, many products based on emulsified fats or oils (condiments, sauces, frozen confections, and others) require long term stability. However, destabilizing emulsions are key to processing raw food materials such as milk and vegetable oils.

search_source.Objectives:
The proposed research aims to develop an integrated two-phase flow boiling/condensation facility for the International Space Station (ISS) to serve as a primary platform for obtaining two-phase flow and heat transfer data in microgravity. By comparing the microgravity data against those obtained in Earth’s gravity, it will be possible to ascertain the influence of body force on two-phase transport phenomena in pursuit of mechanistic models as well as correlations, and to help determine the minimum flow criteria to ensure gravity independent flow boiling and condensation. This research is a joint effort between the Purdue University Boiling and Two-Phase Flow Laboratory (PU-BTPFL) and the NASA Glenn Research Center. Personnel from the two organizations combine extensive experience in research and development of both flow boiling and condensation systems, and in conducting microgravity experiments.

The objectives of the Flow Boiling and the Flow Condensation Experiment (FBCE) in the long duration microgravity environment of the ISS are to:
    1. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity flow boiling critical heat flux (CHF) and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent CHF.
    2. Develop experimentally validated, mechanistic model for microgravity annular condensation and dimensionless criteria to predict minimum flow velocity required to ensure gravity independent annular condensation. Also, develop correlations for other condensation regimes in microgravity.
    3. Obtain flow boiling data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well characterized heating surface as functions of liquid inlet mass velocity and subcooling.
    4. Obtain flow condensation data (heat flux, flow visualization, the wall temperature difference) in long duration microgravity environments for a well-characterized condensing surface as functions of inlet quality and flow rate of condensing vapor. Specific tasks for the study will be as follows.
search_source.Approach:
The approach used in this project is to perform the following sequential series of tasks:
1. Provide detailed design and instrumentation requirements for the Flow Boiling Module (FBM).
2. Provide design and instrumentation requirements for the entire flow loop.
3. Generate test matrix for operating conditions of the study.
4. Perform initial validation tests in both terrestrial gravity and parabolic flight.
5. Perform tests on board the ISS.
6. Based on both the ISS and terrestrial data, develop a series of predictive tools, including empirical correlations as well as theoretical, computational, and machine learning models.
search_source.Hypothesis: In literature spanning many decades, body force in terrestrial gravity is identified as having a profound influence on two-phase transport behavior. This behavior is drastically altered In the absence of gravity, wherein flow fluid and heat transfer are dictated by flow inertia and surface tension. This implies predictive tools from terrestrial gravity studies are inapplicable for design of NASA's reduced gravity systems. This limitation points to a need for performing two-phase flow and heat transfer experiments on board the ISS as basis for formulating relevant reduced gravity predictive tools.
search_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The proposed research will lay the foundation for development of advanced high power to weight ratio thermal management systems for NASA's future space vehicles and planetary bases.  Purdue University research has also shown tremendous value in findings from this projects to numerous other applications including ultra-fast charging of electric vehicles, fusion reactors, hydrogen storage, avionics, high-Mach turbine engines, and advanced electronics in laser, microwave, and radar systems.
